items.objective_statement: discuss possible types and sources of error in any measurement
items.stem: A student repeats a measurement five times and takes the mean. This is done mainly to

options.text: remove a zero error in the instrument

misconception.label: A zero error shifts every reading the same way, so averaging does not remove it.

options.text: reduce the effect of random error

misconception.label: The mean of several readings is not larger than the readings themselves.

options.text: avoid having to use a calibrated instrument

misconception.label: The instrument still has to be calibrated; repeating does not replace that.

steps: A random error makes each reading differ a little from the true value, sometimes high and sometimes low.
Averaging lets the highs and lows cancel.
A systematic error such as a zero error shifts every reading the same way and survives the averaging, so it has to be corrected separately.
solution.answer_line: reduce the effect of random error

items.objective_statement: assess the suitability of instruments on the basis of sensitivity, accuracy and range
items.stem: The range of a measuring instrument is the

options.text: smallest division marked on its scale

misconception.label: The smallest division is the resolution of the scale.

options.text: difference between the largest and smallest readings it can take
smallest change in the quantity it can detect

misconception.label: The smallest detectable change is the sensitivity.

options.text: difference between its reading and the true value

misconception.label: The difference from the true value is the error.

steps: Choosing an instrument means asking three separate questions.
Range asks whether the instrument reaches far enough: can it read the value at all?
Sensitivity asks how small a change it will show, and accuracy asks how close its reading is to the truth.
solution.answer_line: difference between the largest and smallest readings it can take

items.objective_statement: show how derived quantities and their related units are produced
items.stem: The newton is defined as the force that gives a mass of

options.text: 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²
1 kg an acceleration of 10 m s⁻²

misconception.label: 10 m s⁻² is roughly the acceleration of free fall, not the definition of the newton.

options.text: 1 g an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²

misconception.label: The base unit of mass is the kilogram, not the gram.

options.text: 10 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²

misconception.label: The definition uses one kilogram, not ten.

steps: Newton's second law gives F = ma.
Substituting the base units, 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m s⁻².
This is why the newton is called a derived unit.
solution.answer_line: 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻²

items.objective_statement: identify situations in which the application of a force will result in a turning effect
items.stem: A door handle is fitted at the edge of the door rather than near the hinge because this gives

options.text: a smaller moment for the same force

misconception.label: A greater distance gives a greater moment, not a smaller one.

options.text: a larger moment for the same force
a smaller force for the same moment at the hinge

misconception.label: The force applied is the same; it is the moment that changes.

options.text: no change in the turning effect

misconception.label: The turning effect certainly changes with distance; pushing near the hinge barely moves the door.

steps: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
The hinge is the pivot, and the handle is as far from it as the door allows.
So a modest push produces a large turning effect. Pushing close to the hinge needs a much larger force for the same effect.
solution.answer_line: a larger moment for the same force

items.objective_statement: discuss Aristotle's arguments in support of his "law of motion”, that is, v  F"
items.stem: Aristotle held that a steady force is needed to keep a body moving at constant speed. This view is now rejected because

misconception.label: Forces certainly exist; the argument is about what they do.

options.text: a body keeps moving at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it

misconception.label: Constant speed is perfectly possible and is exactly what happens when no resultant force acts.

options.text: friction does not act on a moving body

misconception.label: Friction does act, and it is the reason Aristotle's view looked right.

steps: Everyday experience supports Aristotle: stop pushing a cart and it stops.
It stops because friction acts on it, not because motion needs a force to keep it going.
Remove the friction, as on an air track or in space, and the body carries on at constant velocity with no force at all.
solution.answer_line: a body keeps moving at constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it

items.objective_statement: state Newton's three laws of motion
items.stem: Newton's third law is best stated as

options.text: every action has a larger reaction

misconception.label: The two forces are equal in size, not one larger than the other.

options.text: if A exerts a force on B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A
action and reaction act on the same body and cancel

misconception.label: They act on different bodies, which is exactly why they do not cancel.

options.text: the reaction always follows the action after a short delay

misconception.label: The two forces appear and disappear together, with no delay.

steps: Push on a wall and the wall pushes back on the hand with the same size of force.
The two forces act on different bodies, the wall and the hand.
Because they act on different bodies, they cannot cancel one another; each has its own effect.
solution.answer_line: if A exerts a force on B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A

items.objective_statement: define linear momentum
items.stem: The impulse given to a body is equal to its

misconception.label: Force multiplied by distance gives the change of kinetic energy, not impulse.
Mass times acceleration is the force itself, not the impulse.
Weight is only one possible force, and this holds only if the weight is the resultant force.

steps: Newton's second law can be written as force = change of momentum ÷ time.
Multiplying both sides by the time gives force × time = change of momentum.
The left side is the impulse, so impulse and change of momentum are the same quantity, measured in N s or kg m s⁻¹.
solution.answer_line: change of momentum

items.stem: In a hydroelectric power station the main energy change is from

misconception.label: Electrical energy is the last step, not the first.

items.stem: The gravitational potential energy stored by a body is the energy it has because of its

misconception.label: Energy due to speed is kinetic energy.
Energy due to temperature is internal energy.
Energy stored by changing shape is elastic potential energy.

steps: Lifting a body requires a force to act through a distance, so work is done on it.
That work is stored and can be recovered by letting the body fall.
The store depends on how high the body is above whatever level is being measured from, which is why the level has to be stated.

items.objective_statement: define kinetic energy
items.stem: The kinetic energy of a body depends on its

misconception.label: A stationary body of any mass has no kinetic energy at all.
A fast body of negligible mass carries almost no kinetic energy.
Height belongs to gravitational potential energy.

steps: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because it is moving.
Ek = ½mv², which contains both the mass and the speed.
Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy; doubling the speed makes it four times larger.
solution.answer_line: mass and speed

items.stem: Since h₁ is greater than h₂, liquid P must have a density that is
